p: A reserve like Watatunga rewards a slow, quiet approach. The animals are shy and the space is big, so rushing about won't get you closer to anything. Walk softly, stop often, and give your eyes time to adjust to the long grass and the edges of the woodland; that's when a pair of ears or a curl of horn suddenly appears. Children who are good at spotting games tend to love it, while restless ones might enjoy it more on a guided tour where someone points out the animals.

Time of day matters too. Grazing animals are often more active in the softer light of morning or later afternoon, so if you have a choice of slot, the edges of the day can be rewarding. A pair of binoculars each is a big help, and bring a quiet snack rather than a crinkly multipack if you're planning to linger anywhere.

King's Lynn was once one of England's most important ports and a member of the Hanseatic League, the medieval trading network that linked towns around the North Sea and Baltic. You can still see that heritage in the Hanseatic warehouse buildings and the handsome Custom House on Purfleet Quay. The Stories of Lynn exhibition in the old town hall brings the town's past to life, and True's Yard Fisherfolk Museum tells the story of the North End fishing community. A few miles north-east, Castle Rising has a mighty Norman keep surrounded by huge earthworks that kids love running up and down.

Back in the centre, the Tuesday Market Place and the Saturday Market Place are both framed by grand old buildings, and a riverside walk along the Great Ouse as the light fades is a lovely, unhurried way to end the day.
